claims.text: The as-cast Mg-containing lightweight HEA initially contains a partially supersaturated, metastable Mg-rich solid solution.
The initial alloy contains minor intermetallic phases.
The initial alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
Annealing at approximately 200–500 °C causes stable or partially stable intermetallic phases to nucleate and grow from the Mg-enriched solid solution.
The annealing-induced phase transformation redistributes Mg within the microstructure.
The phase transformation partitions Ti, Al, or Zn between newly formed intermetallics and the surrounding matrix.
Ti-rich surface films can produce passivation and low corrosion current density in Mg-Ti-Zn alloys.
Al or Zn enrichment resulting from the transformation beneficially modifies the passivation-film chemistry.
The transformed local chemistry improves oxide-scale adherence and inhibits oxide spallation.
Intermetallic formation and elemental redistribution reduce micro-galvanic coupling.
The annealed alloy will have a lower corrosion rate than the as-cast alloy because it forms a more protective surface film.
The annealed alloy will exhibit slower high-temperature oxidation kinetics than the as-cast alloy.
The as-cast supersaturated state has a higher corrosion current density than the annealed state.
The oxide scale breaks down more rapidly in the as-cast state than in the annealed state.
The proposed effects are most pronounced at heat-treatment temperatures at or below 500 °C.
Rapid heating or treatment above 500 °C may bypass or alter the intermediate transformation stages.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes electrochemical and thermogravimetric monitoring as concurrent with annealing, whereas the conditions and falsification design place corrosive and oxidizing exposures after annealing. The timing of the environmental measurements is therefore inconsistent.
